In [[numerical mathematics]], '''interval propagation''' or '''interval constraint propagation''' is the problem of contracting interval domains associated to variables of '''R''' without removing any value that is consistent with a set of constraints (i.e., equations or inequalities). It can be used to [[Propagation of uncertainty|propagate uncertainties]] in the situation where [[set estimation|errors are represented by intervals]].<ref>
{{cite book|last1=Jaulin|first1=L.|
last2=Braems|first2=I.|last3=Walter|first3=E.|
title=Interval methods for nonlinear identification and robust control|
year=2002|publisher=In Proceedings of the 41st IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)|
url=http://www.ensta-bretagne.fr/jaulin/cdc02.pdf}}
</ref>  Interval propagation considers an estimation problem as a [[constraint satisfaction]] problem.

== Atomic contractors ==
A contractor associated to an equation involving the variables ''x''<sub>1</sub>,...,''x''<sub>''n''</sub> is an operator which contracts the intervals [''x''<sub>1</sub>],..., [''x''<sub>''n''</sub>] (that are supposed to enclose the ''x''<sub>''i''</sub>'s) without removing any value for the variables that is consistent with the equation.

A contractor is said to be ''atomic'' if it is not built as a composition of other contractors. The main theory that is used to build atomic contractors are based on [[Interval arithmetic|interval analysis]].

'''Example'''. Consider for instance the equation

: <math>
   x_1+x_2 =x_3,
</math>

which involves the three variables ''x''<sub>1</sub>,''x''<sub>2</sub> and ''x''<sub>3</sub>.

The associated contractor is given by the following statements

: <math>
[x_3]:=[x_3] \cap ([x_1]+[x_2])  
</math>

: <math>
[x_1]:=[x_1] \cap ( [x_3]-[x_2])  
</math>

: <math>
[x_2]:=[x_2] \cap ( [x_3]-[x_1])  
</math>

For instance, if 

: <math>
x_1 \in [-\infty ,5], 
</math>

: <math>
x_2 \in [-\infty ,4], 
</math>

: <math>
x_3 \in [ 6,\infty]
</math>

the contractor performs the following calculus

: <math>
x_3=x_1+x_2 \Rightarrow  x_3 \in [6,\infty ] \cap ([-\infty,5]+[-\infty ,4]) =[6,\infty ] \cap [-\infty ,9]=[6,9]. 
</math>

: <math>
x_1=x_3-x_2 \Rightarrow  x_1 \in [-\infty ,5]\cap ([6,\infty]-[-\infty ,4])  =[-\infty ,5] \cap [2,\infty ]=[2,5]. 
</math>

: <math>
x_2=x_3-x_1 \Rightarrow  x_2 \in [-\infty ,4]\cap ([6,\infty]-[-\infty ,5])  = [-\infty ,4] \cap [1,\infty ]=[1,4].
</math>

[[File:Before contraction.gif|thumb|Figure 1: boxes before contraction]]
[[File:After contraction.gif|thumb|Figure 2: boxes after contraction]]

For other constraints, a specific algorithm for implementing the atomic contractor should be written. An illustration is the atomic contractor associated to the equation

: <math>
x_2=\sin(x_1),
</math>

is provided by Figures 1 and 2.

== Decomposition ==
For more complex constraints, a decomposition into atomic constraints (i.e., constraints for which an atomic contractor exists) should be performed. Consider for instance the constraint

: <math>
x+\sin (xy) \leq 0, 
</math>

could be decomposed into

: <math>
a=xy 
</math>

: <math>
b=\sin (a) 
</math>

: <math>
c=x+b.
</math>

The interval domains that should be associated to the new intermediate variables are

: <math>
a \in [-\infty ,\infty ] ,
</math>

: <math>
 b \in [-1 ,1 ] ,
</math>

: <math>
 c \in [-\infty ,0].
</math>

== Propagation ==

The principle of the interval propagation is to call all available atomic contractors until no more contraction could be observed. 
<ref>
{{cite book|last=Cleary|first=J.L.|
title= Logical arithmetic|
year=1987|publisher=Future Computing Systems}}
</ref>
As a result of the [[Knaster-Tarski theorem]], the procedure always converges to intervals which enclose all feasible values for the variables.  A formalization of the interval propagation can be made thanks to the [[interval contractor|contractor algebra]].  Interval propagation converges quickly to the result and can deal with problems involving several hundred of variables.
<ref>
{{cite book|last=Jaulin|first=L.|
title= Localization of an underwater robot using interval constraints propagation|
year=2006|publisher=In Proceedings of CP 2006|
url=http://www.ensta-bretagne.fr/jaulin/redermorcp06.pdf}}
</ref>

== Example ==

Consider the electronic circuit of Figure 3.
[[File:Electronic circuit to illustrate the interval propagation.gif|thumb|Figure 3: File:Electronic circuit to illustrate the interval propagation]] Assume that from different measurements, we know that

: <math>
E \in [23V,26V]
</math>

: <math>
I\in [4A,8A]
</math>

: <math>
U_1 \in [10V,11V]
</math>

: <math>
U_2 \in [14V,17V]
</math>

: <math>
P \in [124W,130W]
</math>

: <math>
R_{1} \in [0 \Omega,\infty ]
</math>

: <math>
R_{2} \in [0 \Omega,\infty ].
</math>

From the circuit, we have the following equations

: <math>
P=EI
</math>

: <math>
U_{1}=R_{1}I
</math>

: <math>
U_{2}=R_{2}I
</math>

: <math>
E=U_{1}+U_{2}.  
</math>

After performing the interval propagation, we get

: <math>
E \in [24V,26V]
</math>

: <math>
I \in [4.769A,5.417A]
</math>

: <math>
U_1 \in [10V,11V]
</math>

: <math>
U_2 \in [14V,16V]
</math>

: <math>
P \in [124W,130W]
</math>

: <math>
R_{1} \in [1.846 \Omega,2.307 \Omega]
</math>

: <math>
 R_{2}\in [2.584 \Omega,3.355 \Omega].
</math>
